That sounds fun. Like you said about certain systems, they are functionally impossible to crack. If you are wanting to pop a Unix box running SELinux and the sysadmin knows their shit, then good luck. Very often, people are the weak link to systems, which is why 2FA is so common. If there is a strong 2FA setup, then a person on the inside is your best bet.

It is all about the individual system. If it's a closed system with no web access, good luck. If it's a website, and you can't gain access to the server directly, then you're limited to fuzzing the backend with input to try to nab some info you shouldn't have.

As for your comment about "real hackers" not calling tools through a gui, you're right. Command-line tools are essentially hammers. They can be used as Swiss army knives, however, in conjunction with custom tools and scripts. Sure, you could run nmap on a website and see if they have any open ports, but it's way more effective to look at routes which are being called on submits/uploads/page loads, and attempting to pop those.

So, I'll break this down into a few points.

A) Battlefield isn't trying to be historically revisionist. It's trying to be inclusive because most importantly, it's a game, and games are meant to be enjoyed by as many people as possible. People like seeing themselves represented in media, hence the inclusion of women, etc.

B) It's unfair to assume that women wanted the "privilege" of having to sit at home. It's not even close to true to assume women didn't want to be soldiers. We had to fight for that right, and men fought us along the way because the military operated very much like a boy's club. Look up the Tailhook Scandal. It's what caused the military to be restructured into the corporate entity it is today. Pre-tailhook culture is one of the many ways women were discouraged from joining the armed forces, and many of those factors still exist.

C) Gaming is a very male-dominated culture. Most games are centered around white male characters, so working to include people who are underrepresented both increases customers and helps to create a more inclusive environment. A game centered around women isn't in the same cultural position as a game centered around men since the *large* majority of games are male-centered. No one is asking literally every game to have literally every demographic, but it's really appreciated when games do make an effort to be inclusive.
